beats.narration_text: Hi — I'm Divij Pawar. This is part one of a two-part series on cross-agent validation. Two AI agents look at the same company. One says revenue grew twelve percent. The other says eight. Which is right? You don't know. I don't know. Neither does the system that produced them. But you do know one of them is wrong.

But one of them is provably wrong — that much is checkable
Correctness needs ground truth. Disagreement needs nothing.

beats.narration_text: Here's the whole idea in one breath. Checking whether an AI's answer is correct needs ground truth you usually don't have. Checking whether two AIs disagree needs nothing at all. So you stop building a truth detector and build a problem detector instead. This half of the video is what the research says that actually takes — and the traps that make naive versions worse than doing nothing.

RIGHT: two agents, two numbers, a set-difference wipe between them — terracotta, labelled DECIDABLE. Then both halves compress into one centred serif line. This is the advance organiser: it names the shape and the stakes, and spends none of the reveals (no ablation, no taxonomy).

beats.act: you cannot check an agent's work
beats.narration_text: Start with the thing nobody wants to say out loud. If an agent hands you a paragraph of confident financial analysis, you have almost no way to check it. You could read its reasoning — but the reasoning is also generated text. A model that confabulated the conclusion will happily confabulate a convincing explanation for it. That's not a rare failure. It's the default: any system graded only by its own output will always look consistent, because consistency is all it was ever asked to produce. The system runs. That was never proof that it's right.

shot.concept: Two movements. First: a clean, well-formatted, plausible agent output fills the frame — professional, cited. Camera pushes into its 'reasoning' section, which greys out under the caption THIS IS ALSO A GENERATED ARTIFACT. Second: the single output multiplies into a grid of six identical, anonymous agent icons — no names, no attribution — each stamping itself CONSISTENT. The grid compresses into one centred line. The point is structural (any self-graded system looks consistent), not a specific incident or named project.

beats.act: ask it twice - and the asymmetry
beats.narration_text: The cheapest version of this is to ask the same model the same question twice, and see if the answers match. That's self-consistency sampling. Its own documentation is blunt: two identical confabulations are still confabulations. High consistency is weak positive evidence. Low consistency is strong negative evidence. Read that asymmetry again — it's what makes the whole field work. Agreement proves almost nothing. Disagreement proves something real, with no ground truth required. But two samples from one model aren't two opinions. They're two draws from one distribution. The fix is to change who answers.

beats.narration_text: Two different agents, compare, flag the mismatch — done? Not quite. Trap one: information asymmetry. Debate seeks truth when agents have seen different evidence. When they've seen the same evidence, it's a persuasion contest — one witness asked twice in two accents. Trap two is worse, because the obvious fix causes it. They disagree, so you average, or add a third agent and vote. But averaging and majority voting amplify shared errors instead of cancelling them. Ensembling only cancels error when errors are independent. A majority of correlated agents is not a majority.

shot.concept: Densest beat in the sheet — two traps, roughly half each; if it needs air, trap two owns the back half. TRAP ONE: two agents reading the SAME document (lines converge to one source), then the same two reading DIFFERENT documents (10-K vs earnings-call transcript). TRAP TWO: three agents, a vote tally, a clean single answer — it deliberately looks good — then replay with all three visibly fed by one shared source, and the 'clean answer' stamps WRONG. Ends on a two-path fork; SURFACE highlighted, RESOLVE dimmed. That fork is reused in B06 — build it as a shared helper so the two beats match exactly. Spacing warning (tips.txt section 6): three agent nodes with chips underneath collide at floor type size — wrap 'MAJORITY VOTE' to two lines or widen the node spacing.

beats.act: four kinds of disagreement, and staged detection
beats.narration_text: Once you're detecting disagreement instead of resolving it, most disagreements turn out to be boring. The literature sorts them four ways. Stylistic — same substance, different words. Noise; flag it and you'll cry wolf. Reasoning — different paths, different conclusions. That's the real thing. High-confidence disagreement — both sure, mutually exclusive. Surface it; don't synthesize a false consensus. And adversarial — agents faking agreement. Then, staged detection: a cheap classifier handles about seventy-three percent of pairs with no model call. Only the uncertain ones escalate. Sixty-two percent lower cost, ninety point eight percent accuracy held. A check you can afford to run on everything beats a better check you run on a sample.

Numbers in PT Mono (data job). Card labels are chips — auto_box every one; 'HIGH-CONFIDENCE DISAGREEMENT' is 28 chars and will overflow a hand-sized rectangle, so wrap it to two lines. beats.act: the ablation, and the fork in the road
beats.narration_text: So what does the mature version of this look like? The most complete systems in the research run many specialized agents across multiple phases, evaluated on hundreds of questions. One published ablation study tells you what actually matters. Remove the adversarial debate, and faithfulness drops zero point one one nine — the largest drop by far. Remove the elegant source-weighting matrix, and it costs zero point zero zero six. Nothing. The sophisticated machinery is the least important part. What matters is having something whose job is to disagree. That system then resolves the disagreement. But arbitration needs heterogeneity you can verify. If you can't prove your agents fail independently, arbitration hides your only evidence that something's wrong. So surface it instead. Machines verify conformance. Humans verify adequacy.

Only the -0.119 bar takes terracotta; the -0.006 bar is drawn almost invisibly short next to it — the size contrast IS the argument, do not annotate it further. (3) The B04 fork returns, identical geometry, and this time SURFACE locks in. Closes on the constitution line in EB Garamond, held with no motion. beats.narration_text: So, part one in four lines. Correctness needs ground truth. Disagreement doesn't. Different evidence matters more than a different model. Never resolve what you can't prove is independent. And a cheap check that runs on everything beats a better one that runs on a sample.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude: "Take two AI agents I already run. What different evidence would each need to see for their disagreement to mean something about the world, instead of something about my prompt?" That's the information-asymmetry trap, aimed at your own stack. Look for whether Claude can name two genuinely different sources — if it can't, you don't have two witnesses, you have one witness asked twice. Part two: the code.
